Restore Solomon's Temple

During the Event the Glory of the Temple Mound was caught in the storm of the apocalypse leaving Mizoram faithful directionless in the sea of chaos that followed the Event. Now that the faithful of Kohhran Thianghlim have returned home grander than ever before an ambitious lord such as yourself can build a grand temple to God like the one raised by King Solomon himself.
Unify the Holy Church

With Solomon's Temple Restored, many weary faithful look to you for guidance awaiting your word. The ministries that were once disunited look to you as the Grand Reverend of God himself and request that you guide the faithful with your own steady hand.

Construction of the Third Temple will begin immediately on the outskirts of Aizawl. The design of the new temple is greater in scope than the previous church on the site or even King Solomon's fabled First Temple. Your architects estimate that the construction will take roughly four years. When it is finished, it will truly be a sight to see!
Our people need but wait a little longer.
The Third Temple, The Holy Church

The First Temple, built by King Solomon, was destroyed by the invading Babylonians. The Second Temple, built under the auspices of Cyrus the Great of Persia, was razed by the Romans after a terrible siege. The Third Temple, first seen in the dreams of Lalbiakmawia Sailo and built by the great [FromFrom.GetTitledFirstName] in Mizoram, shall stand for all eternity!\n\nThe magnificent building has become a dominant feature of Aizawl, instantly recognizable from far away by travelers approaching the city. Truly, Solomon himself would have been moved to tears by the sight.
It is beautiful.
The Future of the Church

The Proud Restoration of Solomon's Temple was quickly followed by disparate ministries of Kohhran Thianghlim declaring you as the Grand Reverend to hold the steady hand of the church so that this proud realm may last until the day that Jesus returns to usher in the millenia Kingdom of Heaven and collect the faithful in his realm.
Long live the Reverend, Glory to the Church!
An interesting development...

Mortification of the Flesh is an act undertaken in order to repent for sins or as a way to share and imitate the Passion of Christ. While the tradition long predates the event, it was only after it that it took the more extreme form practiced by contemporary Penitentes, as instruments of mortification were made bloodier. Penitente Rulers are expected to practice mortification regularly..
I will walk barefoot and wear the Cilice.

Self-flagellation is seen as very pious, however it also carries more risk than simply wearing the Cilice.

You arrive in Rome, the place where Saints Peter and Paul were martyred during the reign of Emperor Nero, and where the Pope, the leader of the entire Catholic Church, used to reside. You walk through the city's crowded streets, passing ancient churches that reflect over 2,000 years of history. Along the way, you say your prayers quietly, thanking God for the grace of reaching this place. Soon you enter St. Peter's Square, where the Pope used to bless pilgrims, and proceed to the Sistine Chapel. There, you kneel and begin your silent, humble prayer.

You arrive in Fatima, an unassuming Portuguese city that nonetheless witnessed one of the most famous Marian apparitions, where the Blessed Virgin Mary appeared to three children: Francisco, Jacinta, and Lucia. This apparition, recognized by the Church, contributed to the flourishing of devotion to the Immaculate Heart of Our Lady and brought many spiritual fruits. Entering Fatima, you head towards the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Fatima, which was rebuilt after the Event during the reign of King Sancho. You enter and see the statue of Our Lady of Fatima
column3: it is more beautiful than you could have imagined. As is customary, you pray the rosary before the altar in the chapel and then leave to spend some time in this place.

column2: You arrive in Munich, the capital of Bavaria, where years ago the good King Albert decided to march on pagan Italy and liberate it from the superstitions of polytheism, thus becoming the first post-event Roman emperor. The first Christian episcopal see was founded here in the 8th century at the initiative of Saint Boniface, a Benedictine monk, and in the 19th century, the diocese was elevated to an archbishopric. As you walk through the streets of this city, they remind you of events, some more mysterious, some more peaceful, some less so. Soon you reach Marienplatz, named after the Blessed Virgin Mary, where the town hall and the Mariensäule—a column built in the 17th century in honor of Mary—are located. Soon you reach the coveted Cathedral of Our Lady, built in Gothic and Renaissance styles. You go inside and see beautiful pearls of sacred art, you go deeper and soon you see the image of the coronation of the Blessed Virgin Mary as Queen of Heaven and Earth, you kneel before this image and begin to pray to Mary, thanking her for the grace of reaching this city.

You arrive in Jerusalem, the holy city, the capital of the ancient kingdom of Israel, the city where Jesus Christ taught and was crucified. This city is unique because, unlike Rome, it is sacred both to Jews who do not recognize Christ as the messiah and to Muslims who do not recognize Jesus Christ as God. You walk through the streets of Jerusalem, crowded as usual, filled with people from all over the world. You pass ancient churches, both Catholic and Orthodox, Jewish and Muslim. After a while, you leave the city and head to Mount Golgotha, where Jesus Christ was crucified over 2,500 years ago. As you ascend the mountain, you kneel and, like other pilgrims before and after you, pray in silence.

You arrive in Nazareth. This where, centuries ago, our Savior Jesus Christ was raised under the watchful eye of St. Joseph and the Blessed Virgin Mary. From afar, you see many ancient churches – the Basilica of the Annunciation, St. Joseph's Church, the Church of the Archangel Gabriel, and other sacred sites. You choose one of the churches, walk the same streets that existed over 2,000 years ago, and enter the church as one of the pilgrims. You cross yourself with holy water and kneel before the altar to begin your silent, pilgrim prayer.

You arrive in Lourdes, a small and unassuming French town in southwestern France. It was here that the Blessed Virgin Mary herself appeared to Saint Bernadette Soubirous, revealing the fact of her Immaculate Conception. This apparition was one of the most important, as it contributed to the proclamation of the dogma of the Immaculate Conception by Blessed Pope Pius IX. You head towards the Basilica of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, and upon reaching it, you are met with the sight of an incredibly beautiful church. You enter and wander the church, admiring the beautiful stained-glass windows. After a while, you kneel and quietly recite the rosary, thanking Our Lady of Lourdes for helping you reach this place.

You arrive in Canterbury, a place of importance to English Catholics and Anglicans as the first Christian episcopal see in England, headed by Saint Augustine of Canterbury as its first bishop. Although Canterbury in Kent is not the largest city in the region, it still impresses with its appearance and historic character, as evidenced by the old pre-event buildings. You pass such ancient structures as Canterbury Town Hall, built during the reign of Richard II, and reach Canterbury Cathedral, the site of the death of Archbishop of Canterbury Thomas Becket, venerated as a saint by Catholics and Anglicans alike. You enter the cathedral, observe the beautiful work of Romanesque-Gothic architecture inside, and when you reach the balustrade, you kneel and begin to pray silently.

You arrive in York, a place of importance to both Anglicans and English Catholics. It was here that in the 7th century, Saint Paulinus of York, a common saint for Catholics, Orthodox, and Anglicans, served as bishop. In the 8th century, York was merely a bishopric, but in the 8th century it was elevated to the rank of archbishopric, becoming the second most important episcopal see in the Kingdom of England. Entering York, you pass historic streets that remember better times before the Event, old churches like the Church of the Holy Trinity in Goodramgate and the Church of St. Martin le Grand, before reaching York Cathedral. It is a beautiful monument of sacred architecture, built in the Gothic style. You enter and are dazzled by the sight of beautiful sculptures, bas-reliefs, and stained glass windows. You walk deeper into the cathedral, and when you are closer to the altar than further away, you kneel and begin to pray, thanking God for the grace of reaching such a beautiful church.

You have finally arrived at Constantinople, Queen of Cities and the former seat of the Roman Empire. Before you rises an immense and ancient metropolis whose towering walls, crowded harbors, and countless domes dwarf every city you have seen upon your pilgrimage. As you make your way through the winding streets in search of lodging, your senses are overcome by the cries of merchants, the mingling scents of incense and spice, and the endless throngs of travelers and sailors from every corner of Christendom. Along your path appear ancient churches, monasteries, and monuments adorned with holy icons and relics of the saints, each bearing witness to the city’s long and sacred history. Like any devout pilgrim, you press onward through the bustling crowds with eager anticipation, longing at last to behold such renowned and venerable sanctuaries as the Hagia Sophia and the Church of Saint George, and to offer prayers of thanksgiving before their holy altars in glorification of God for safely guiding you upon your journey.

You have finally arrived at Constantinople, now ruled by the Muslim Sultans though still filled with the memory of its ancient Christian history. Before you rises an immense and ancient metropolis whose towering walls, crowded harbors, and countless domes dwarf every city you have seen upon your pilgrimage. As you make your way through the winding streets in search of lodging, your senses are overcome by the cries of merchants, the mingling scents of incense and spice, and the endless throngs of travelers and sailors from far and wide. Along your path stand the ancient ruins of churches, monasteries, and monuments, many transformed to serve the new rulers or left to rot yet they still bear witness to the city’s long and sacred history. Like any devout pilgrim, you press onward through the bustling crowds with solemn wonder and anticipation, longing at last to behold the Patriarchal Cathedral of St. George and the ancient once Cathedral of Hagia Sophia though lost to the faith, and to offer prayers to God amidst the fading remnants of New Rome’s once-glorious Christian inheritance.

You have finally arrived at Constantinople, now taken by foreign infidels though still filled with the memory of its ancient Christian history. Before you rises an immense and ancient metropolis whose towering walls, crowded harbors, and countless domes dwarf every city you have seen upon your pilgrimage. As you make your way through the winding streets in search of lodging, your senses are overcome by the cries of merchants, the mingling scents of incense and spice, and the endless throngs of travelers and sailors from far and wide. Along your path stand the ancient ruins of churches, monasteries, and monuments, many transformed to serve the new rulers or left to rot yet they still bear witness to the city’s long and sacred history. Like any devout pilgrim, you press onward through the bustling crowds with solemn wonder and anticipation, longing at last to behold the Patriarchal Cathedral of St. George and the ancient once Cathedral of Hagia Sophia though lost to the faith, and to offer prayers to God amidst the fading remnants of New Rome’s once-glorious Christian inheritance.

You arrive in the peninsula of Holy Athos. In the distance, you see the ancient Monastery of the Great Lavra, founded over a millennium ago by the great saint Athanasios. As you walk closer to the Lavra, you hear the blessed hymns recounting the tradition of the Mountain all the way back to its earliest foundations of the Blessed Virgin’s trip with the Apostle John the Evangelist to visit her Son’s friend, Lazarus, on Cyprus, where she would be blown off course to the then-pagan Athos. The Blessed Virgin would walk ashore and be overwhelmed by the mountain’s wonderful and wild natural beauty. Then she blessed it and asked her Son for it to be her garden. And a voice was heard saying, “Let this place be your inheritance and your garden, a paradise and a haven of salvation for those seeking to be saved.” Like any devout pilgrim, you dwell on this blessed tradition and are brought to prayer in glorification of the Lord.

You arrive in Arkhangelsk, a city in northern Russia named after St. Michael the Archangel. It's a frosty and inhospitable area, yet it holds many spiritual treasures for Old Believers. As you enter the city, you see a multitude of people: merchants from distant lands and local sailors alike. You greet them and continue your journey until you reach the Cathedral of St. Elijah, a local cathedral built in the 18th century. This place is a place of special devotion to St. Elijah among Orthodox Christians, so you head there too. You wander through the old streets until you reach the cathedral. You enter and encounter beautiful icons and paintings. You continue your journey until you see a beautiful icon of St. Elijah. You kneel for a day and pray to this saint to obtain favors from your God.

You arrive in Chartres, a significant spiritual site for French Catholics and Gallicans, a place where many pilgrimages took place before the Event, as it is said that the shroud of the Virgin Mary is located there. You enter the city and quickly head towards the Cathedral of Our Lady. You pass other pilgrims and ordinary merchants who have come to the city for business. Soon you reach the cathedral's doors, gaze intently at it, admiring its Gothic beauty. You enter, kneel before the main altar, and head to the Chapel of the Martyrs. When you arrive, you see the shroud displayed. You kneel before it and begin to pray to Mary, thanking her for granting you the grace to come to this place.

You arrive in Esztergom, an important city for Hungarian Catholics and Coronites. It was here in 1001 that the first episcopal see located in Hungary was established, making Esztergom the eternal center of Christianity in Hungary, especially since the Archbishops of Esztergom long ago received the privilege of coronating every Hungarian king. Walking through this old town, you pass ancient streets and merchants from Austria, Slovakia, Romania, and Yugoslavia. Soon you reach the Primate's Basilica of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary and St. Adalbert, the seat of each Archbishop of Esztergom, built in a beautiful, classical style. Enter and behold the splendor of this divine temple, built centuries ago by the pious King of Hungary, St. Stephen. You walk towards the main altar and stop in front of the chancel, immersing yourself in silent prayer.

You arrive in Jasna Gora. In the distance, on a hill, you see an ancient monastery built here in time immemorial. You walk closer – you pass monks in white habits praying and walk to the holiest place here – the Chapel of Our Lady of Czestochowa. There, you see a beautiful sight – beautiful antediluvian altars, ancient walls, and the main altar, which, along with the chancel, is separated from the congregation by beautifully crafted bars. But behind these bars lies an image of Our Lady of Czestochowa, just as beautiful as you imagined, according to legend, created by the apostle St. Luke himself. You kneel before this image and, like any devout pilgrim, begin to pray.

You arrive in Lund, a city no longer small, but one of significance in the history of Christianity. Lund is no ordinary town, but the seat of the first episcopal see in Sweden, which, at the beginning of the spread of the Christian faith in this region, encompassed all of Sweden and Norway. As it was, Lund is not a crowded city, so you easily navigate the streets and reach your destination: St. Lawrence's Cathedral, a monument to Romanesque architecture in Scandinavia. You enter the cathedral, realizing you are entering one of the oldest buildings in the city. You pass through the church and stop near the balustrade. Then you kneel, fold your hands in silent prayer, and begin to pray to God, thanking Him for the grace of bringing you here.

You arrive in Nitra, the spiritual center of Slovak Christianity. It was here that the first bishopric in Slovakia was established, thanks to the efforts of the holy missionaries, St. Cyril and Methodius, who sought to spread the light of Christ to the Slavic nations. Inspired by the story of St. Cyril and Methodius, you walk through the streets of this city until you reach St. Emmeram's Cathedral. You enter in your pilgrim's rags and are captivated by the sight of sacred art. However, you are not here to feast your eyes – you go deeper into the church, kneel, and begin your humble prayer.

You arrive in Orleans, where Saint Joan of Arc, the Maid of Orleans and national heroine of France, lived for a time. It is also home to the Cathedral of the Holy Cross, where Saint Joan of Arc prayed during the English siege of the city. As you wander the streets of the city, you soon come across Joan of Arc's house where she lived. You enter the house and pray before the icon of Joan of Arc installed there. Then you go to the Cathedral of the Holy Cross, built in the Gothic style, and enter, observing its majesty. As you approach the chancel, you kneel and immerse yourself in silent prayer.

You arrive in Plock, an old Polish city that, paradoxically, didn't outshine Warsaw or Gdañsk in size and popularity before the Event. However, after the Event, something previously ignored was noticed here – according to tradition, this is where Saint Maria Francisca Kozlowska was born, taught, and died in the odor of holiness – a fact that made Plock a center of pilgrimage. Like other pilgrims, you head to the same place – the Cathedral of Mercy and Love – the first Mariavite cathedral. You pass other pilgrims and enter the cathedral, adjacent to an ancient monastery. Inside, other pilgrims are already gathered, ready to immerse themselves in prayer...

You arrive in Pustozersk, a unique place, for here once stood a town where Saint Avvakum Petrov was imprisoned for many years and burned at the stake in 1682. When you reach this place, you see no houses
column3: the village has been defunct for many years, having been abandoned even before the Event. But this field has not ceased to be sacred to Old Believers. It is what Rome is to Catholics, the site of the greatest martyrdom, the martyrdom of the Russian Saint Peter, who was the progenitor of the faith on this land, its defender, and martyr. As one of many Old Believers, you find a chapel where, according to tradition, Avvakum was burned, and you place a candle and say a prayer in honor of this martyr.

column2: You arrive in Riga, the capital of the Latvian nation and the eastern outpost of Lutheranism for many years. The origins of Christianity date back to the city's founding in 1201 by the Catholic Livonian Order. In 1522, Riga formally became Protestant. Upon entering Riga, you see the old city, which, despite the events, has retained its status as one of the heartlands of Baltic trade. On your way to the local cathedral, you pass the House of the Blackhead and continue until you reach the Cathedral of the Blessed Virgin Mary. You enter and walk deeper into the church, and when you reach the chancel, you stop before it and join your hands in prayer in honor of the Triune God.

You arrive in Saragossa, one of the largest cities in Spain, but also one of the most important for Spanish Catholics and beyond. It is here, according to tradition, that the first Marian apparition took place, occurring while Mary was still alive. When St. James the Apostle was on the verge of discouragement, seeing very little fruit from his mission, Mary appeared to him, accompanied by thousands of angels. She stood on a marble column and gave the Apostle her likeness, requesting the construction of a chapel in its honor, to which the Apostle agreed. Upon entering Saragossa, you enter a maze of streets, but after a while you find your way to the Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar. You enter, and when you reach the chancel, you stop, kneel, and begin to pray to Mary, thanking her for obtaining from God the grace to come here.

You arrive in Seville, one of the most famous cities in the Mediterranean, and the site of the Cathedral of Our Lady, considered one of the greatest churches in Christianity. It took many years to build, starting in 1434, and was only completed in 1506, consecrated in 1507. Entering Seville, you pass ancient streets and people from the cold north, the Orient, and Africa. Soon, you arrive near the Cathedral, greeted by the sight of La Giralda, the cathedral's bell tower, which was once a minaret. You walk towards the cathedral and arrive at its doors, enter through them, and describe the cathedral's ornate and majestic interior. As you approach the chancel, you stop, kneel, and fall into prayer, thanking God for the grace of reaching this magnificent temple.

You arrive in Szekesfehervar, the coronation site of the ancient kings of Hungary. Legend has it that this is the tomb of Saint Stephen, the first Christian king of Hungary, who, according to the Coronites, received the Sacra Corona from Pope Sylvester. You walk through the streets of this town, heading towards the ruins of the old cathedral of Szekesfehervar. When you arrive, you see the remains of the old cathedral, destroyed by the Turks over 1,000 years ago. You imagine the cathedral's splendor, approach the bricks, kneel, and touch them, and after a moment, you begin your silent prayer to Saint Stephen to obtain God's graces.

You arrive in Turku, a city important to many Finns as the spiritual center of Christianity in Finland. The capital of the Diocese of Finland was moved to this city in the 13th century, and it was proclaimed metropolitan in the 19th century. Entering the city, you pass old streets and churches, noting that despite the horrors of the Event, the city has survived in better condition than Stockholm or Uppsala. You soon find your way to Turku Cathedral, a church built in a blend of Romanesque and Gothic styles. You enter this church and walk deeper into its interior – beautiful frescoes painted in the 19th century depicting biblical scenes and two important events: the baptism of the first Finns and the presentation of the Finnish translation of the Bible by Mikael Agricola to Gustav Vasa. You pass successive columns of this church and arrive near the chancel, where you stop and kneel to pay homage to God in silent prayer.

You arrive in Utrecht, a Dutch city, one of the largest in the region, a place where, before the Event, the archbishops of this place rebelled against papal authority and welcomed the spiritual sons of Maria Francisca, making them their brothers in the episcopate. You pass through the streets of Utrecht and the merchants, officials, and beggars who walk them. You soon reach St. Gertrude's Cathedral – this is where the turning point occurred, when the Archbishop of Utrecht ordained young Mariavites as bishops and commissioned them to spread the true faith in Poland. You kneel in the cathedral and begin to pray silently, knowing that somewhere in this cathedral lie the bones of saint bishops.

You arrive in Vilnius, the Lithuanian capital, but also an important place for Mariavites and other local christians. You walk with other pilgrims to this one place – not the cathedral, not the Basilian abbey (although pilgrims also go to them, just secondarily), but to an inconspicuous gate – known as the Gate of Dawn. There, you see the goal of your journey – the Gate of Dawn, and above it, a painting of Our Lady of the Gate of Dawn. You kneel before the painting on the side of the street, take out your rosary, and begin to pray as pilgrim tradition dictates.

You arrive in Wadowice. Less popular pilgrimage site, mainly due to the small size of the town itself. It's not a metropolis like Vilnius or Rome, but a modest town, still home to places built before the Event, where people once lived, but now only animals. You pass through the ruined Wadowice, the birthplace of Saint Pope John Paul II, a great Pole and bishop. You first visit the old parish – the Basilica of the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, then the house next door, considered the family home of the holy pope. Then you proceed towards the former Carmelite Monastery. You walk, passing old houses, and crossing the threshold of monasteries. You see beautiful side altars, more beautiful than those in the main church in the market square. You kneel and pay homage to God, as pilgrimage tradition dictates.

You arrive in Vyatskoye, a traditional Old Believer community near Uglich. It was here that they gathered during the horrors of the Event, and here they survived the worst. Despite the later return of New Believers to these lands, they survived in this small settlement. You enter and see old sheds
column3: time has stood still here. You continue walking and reach the local parish, enter, kneel, and then begin to pray, thanking God for the grace to reach this place.

column2: You arrive in Wittenberg, where Doctor Martin Luther, the Augustinian monk and founder of Lutheranism, lived and worked. This city wouldn't be so famous if Martin Luther hadn't nailed his 95 theses to the door of the local All Saints' Church. You walk through the city's streets, past buildings, and arrive at the goal of your pilgrimage, the church itself. Above the door, you see a painting depicting Martin Luther and Philipp Melanchthon kneeling before the Crucified Christ. You enter and walk, past sculptures gazing at you from afar, see ornate frescoes, and when you get close to the altar, you stop, kneel, and pray silently, contemplating your misery and the majesty of God.

You arrive in Kyiv, the cradle of Christianity in Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus. It was here that the first episcopal see in these lands was established when Vladimir the Great converted and accepted baptism from Constantinople. For hundreds of years, Kyiv held a leading role among Russian Orthodox Christians until the establishment of the Patriarchate in Moscow. Even today, this city remains important to Russian Orthodoxy as the place where Rus' was baptized and where it was liberated from the errors of paganism. Soon after, you pass many churches in this city and reach the most important of them, Saint Sophia's Cathedral, which, according to legend, existed even before Saint Vladimir's baptism, making it the oldest church in this part of the world. You enter the cathedral, observe beautiful mosaics and frescoes depicting saints, and marvel at their beauty until you reach the chancel and the altar, which is covered by an iconostasis. You stop and begin to pray silently to God for the grace to get here.

You arrive in Budapest, the ancient capital of the Kingdom of Hungary and the site of St. Stephen's Basilica, the largest cathedral in Hungary, which can accommodate over 8,000 worshippers. You walk through the streets of this ancient, pre-event capital, passing merchants, priests, and locals, passing smaller churches and historic buildings, until you reach the aforementioned Basilica. You enter this magnificent church. In the center, you see the beautiful main altar with its angelic appearance. You kneel before it, pray for a moment, and soon you reach one of the side chapels, where the relic of one of Hungary's greatest saints, St. Stephen, is kept—his right hand. When you find this chapel, you kneel before the relic and begin to pray the chaplet to Saint Stephen.

You arrive in Walsingham, an unassuming village in East Anglia with a rich history. Years ago, apparitions took place here, in which the Blessed Virgin Mary commanded the construction of a replica of the house of the Holy Family in Nazareth, which was done. A statue of the Virgin Mary was erected in the replica. Soon, this place became a site of many pilgrimages in England, as it was believed that anyone who came here would not be denied their request. The statue was destroyed on the orders of Henry VIII, but despite this, a new one was built, and it still attracts pilgrims to this day. Remembering this history, you walk as a pilgrim through the village, passing cottages, and when you reach the sanctuary, you enter, cross yourself, and approach the statue of Our Lady. Founded in the 7th century as an abbey of the Order of St. Benedict, from William the Conqueror until the Event, it was the site of coronations of the Kings of England and later Great Britain. This church changed hands many times, sometimes as a Catholic church, sometimes as an Anglican church, and sometimes under other owners. You enter, and as you enter, you realize that this Abbey is not only one of the largest churches but also a cemetery: over 3,000 distinguished individuals of England are buried beneath it. One by one, you visit each chapel, gazing at these works of sacred architecture, whose purpose was to worship God. Soon, you conclude your journey, amazed by the beauty and richness of this church.

You arrive in Glastonbury, an ancient abbey built long ago and destroyed during the reign of Henry VIII. As you reach the ancient ruins of this monastery, you see that little remains of its former glory, yet you somehow feel that it still lives on, that it has not been forgotten not only by Christians but also by non-Christians. You slowly walk around these ruins, pondering the issues of transience and death, as well as the story of the martyrdom of the monastery's last abbot.
